back: Expiration removes entries past their TTL (freshness). Eviction removes entries because the cache is full (capacity).
One-off entries (scans, crawlers, batch jobs) pushing out entries that would have been reused.
Least recently used: evict the entry whose last access is oldest. Each hit moves an entry to the most-recent end.
Scans: reading many keys once makes them all 'recent' and flushes the hot set.

front: How do databases make LRU scan-resistant?
back: InnoDB inserts new pages at the middle of its LRU list; PostgreSQL uses clock-sweep with usage counts.

front: Two structures in an O(1) LRU cache?
back: A hash map from key to node, and a doubly linked list of nodes in recency order.
To unlink a node in O(1) you need its previous neighbour; a singly linked list needs an O(n) walk to find it.

front: Why sentinel head and tail nodes?
back: They're never removed, so insert and unlink never have to handle an empty list or null neighbours.

front: Why is a shared LRU hard under high concurrency?
back: Every get mutates the list, so every access needs a lock. Libraries shard the cache or buffer access updates.
Least frequently used: evict the entry with the lowest access count. Resists scans.
It never forgets old popularity (needs decay), and new entries start with the lowest count so they're evicted first.
Caffeine's policy: a small recency window plus a compact frequency sketch that decides whether a new entry may displace an old one.

front: Advantage of FIFO and random over LRU?
back: Nothing to update on a hit, so no lock or list shuffle per read; cheap and easy to make concurrent.
noeviction: once maxmemory is reached, writes that need memory fail with an error.
allkeys-lru can evict any key; volatile-lru only evicts keys that have a TTL set.
It samples maxmemory-samples keys (default 5), evicts the one idle longest, and keeps a small pool of candidates between rounds.
